welcome_lead: Meet the Birlings, the Inspector and the Britain of 1912 — written in 1945.
meta_desc: GCSE English Literature — An Inspector Calls foundations: Priestley, characters, context.
final_note: You mapped the Birling family, Inspector Goole and the gap between 1912 setting and 1945 audience.

concepts.def: Drama designed to teach a moral lesson
Belief in shared wealth and collective responsibility
Economic system based on private profit
Mysterious figure who interrogates the Birlings
Working-class woman whose suicide drives the plot
When the audience knows more than a character

walkthroughs.body_html:
Priestley wrote An Inspector Calls in 1945 but set it in 1912.

His 1945 audience had just lived through two world wars and the Great Depression. Watching the smug 1912 Birlings, they know catastrophe is coming — that gap is the play's engine.

Arthur Birling: capitalist patriarch. Sybil Birling: cold, class-snob mother. Sheila: changes — symbol of younger generation. Eric: privileged drinker who fathers Eva's child. Gerald Croft: old-money fiancé.

Each represents a slice of Edwardian Britain — and a different reaction to responsibility.

The Inspector arrives just as Birling declares 'a man has to mind his own business.'

His name 'Goole' sounds like 'ghoul' — supernatural? Moral conscience? Mouthpiece for Priestley? He leaves with the warning of 'fire and blood and anguish' — a threat 1945 audiences recognised.

mcqs.q: In what year is An Inspector Calls SET?
What does the Inspector's surname 'Goole' suggest?

numericals.q: How many members of the Birling family does the Inspector interrogate?
numericals.hint: Arthur, Sybil, Sheila, Eric — and Gerald the fiancé makes five total.
